title: Boxes with walls, and the dice game in a second tongue
summary: Give every box in C++ a promise about what it will hold, march an int off the two billion cliff and record what your own compiler did, then rebuild the season 1 dice game in the stricter language.
materials: the laptop with g++ and the editor a parent installed and tested before the season
the bug diary, open at the Error Bestiary chapter started in week 1
the season 1 dice game: the MakeCode share link, or its rules written on paper
paper and pencil for the plan that gets translated
the min-max thermometer outside, for the 30 second dawn reading

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop first: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: last week the compiler read your whole program before it would run a single line of it. Today the question is what it was reading for. A large part of the answer is types.

Imagine: in Python you write n = 5 and Python works out what n is. In C++ you write int n = 5, and that is a promise. This box holds a whole number, nothing else, ever. The language holds you to your word, and it checks the promise before the program runs at all.

A promise like that buys speed, because the machine knows exactly how much room to set aside and never has to ask again. It also costs something, and the cost is the whole of today: a box with a fixed size has walls. Python numbers grow as big as they like. A C++ int does not.

Plan, part one: four boxes and their promises. int for whole numbers, long long for whole numbers far too big for an int, double for numbers with a decimal point, string for text. Print what each one can hold, then march an int off the edge on purpose and write down exactly what your own machine did.

Plan, part two: Rosetta. Your oldest program is the shake-to-roll dice game from season 1: roll two numbers from 1 to 6, the higher number wins, a tie is worth something. That plan does not change today. Only the costume changes. Nothing about the game gets better in C++, and saying that out loud is part of the exercise. The algorithm is the thing. The language is what it is wearing.

One rule that started last week and holds for the rest of the season: your hands, your keyboard. A grown-up may watch, and may be asked a question, and does not type.

Five minutes, hands on the home row, eyes on the screen. Today's words are the ones this week's code needs: include, int, long, double, string, cout, main, return, seed, roll. Type each word five times.

Then type this line three times without looking down, landing the semicolon every single time:

std::cout << n << "\n";

The two colons are one key pressed twice, and they are how C++ says which cupboard a name came from. cout lives in the cupboard called std.

figure.alt: Three C++ boxes of fixed size, side by side. An int is 4 bytes, 32 switches, holding up to 2,147,483,647. A long long is 8 bytes, 64 switches, holding a far bigger number. A double is 8 bytes and holds numbers with a decimal point. Every size is fixed once and for all when the program compiles, unlike a Python number, which grows itself a bigger box as needed.

steps.title: Memory is a street of fixed-size boxes
steps.body:
Ask the machine how big its boxes are. Put this line inside a program and run it:

std::cout << sizeof(int) << ' ' << sizeof(long long) << ' ' << sizeof(double) << '\n';

On a laptop like yours those print 4, 8 and 8. Those are bytes, and on your machine a byte is eight switches, each one either off or on. So an int is a house with 32 switches in it and a long long is a house with 64.

Here is why the number of switches matters. With 32 switches there are exactly 2 to the 32nd different patterns, which is 4294967296 of them. An int has to hold negative numbers too, so it spends about half its patterns on those. What is left is 2147483647 as the biggest number it can hold, and 2147483648 below zero as the smallest.

Now the part worth remembering. C++ does not promise those sizes. It promises that an int is at least 16 switches wide and a long long at least 64. Your compiler chose 32 for int, and sizeof is how you ask it instead of assuming. A different machine can give a different answer to the same question, which is why you ask.

Python never made you choose, because a Python whole number is not a fixed house at all. It grows itself a bigger one whenever the number outgrows the old one. That is a real convenience, and it has a real price, and today you meet the price.

figure.alt: A screw in cross-section: a steel core inside a thin zinc coating. Zinc reacts with oxygen before the steel underneath does, sacrificing itself first, which is why a galvanized screw resists rust. A magnet held nearby still pulls the screw whether the zinc coating is shiny or the surface has rusted, because the iron underneath is magnetic either way.

items.s: coating scratched: steel underneath can rust

steps.title: Rust is a slow fire, and why some screws avoid it
steps.body:
Rust is iron reacting with oxygen and water to form iron oxide, and it is a close chemical cousin of burning. Both are a metal or fuel combining with oxygen and releasing energy, just at wildly different speeds. Burning is that reaction in seconds. Rusting is the same idea stretched over months or years.

Bare steel screws left outside will rust visibly within weeks in damp air. That is why so many hardware screws, including the ones in your kit, come galvanized: coated in a thin layer of zinc. Zinc reacts with oxygen before the steel underneath gets the chance, sacrificing itself first. It keeps protecting a scratch in the coating for a while even after bare steel is exposed.

Check it with the kit's magnet, kept well away from phones, credit cards and laptops, which a strong magnet can damage. Both a shiny zinc-coated screw and a rusted one should still pull to it, since the iron underneath either coating is still iron. Rust changes the surface, not the metal's magnetism.

figure.alt: A number line showing an int marching toward its ceiling: 2147483645, then 2147483646, then 2147483647, the biggest number an int can hold. One more step walks off the cliff into undefined behaviour, printing whatever large negative number this machine happened to choose, since C++ makes no promise about what happens past the edge.

steps.title: Bug diary, and three more for the Bestiary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time, and what you tried. The Bestiary chapter takes the ones the compiler caught, written in your words rather than its own.

Three worth breaking on purpose today.

Leave the semicolon off the end of a line. The compiler complains about a semicolon, but it often blames the line after the one you broke, because that is where it noticed. Write down which line it blamed.

Write cout instead of std::cout. The compiler tells you the name was not declared here, and some versions then suggest what you probably meant.

Try std::string s = "5"; s = s + 3;. This one is refused because there is no version of plus that takes a string on the left and a whole number on the right.

The exact wording of all three differs between compilers, and even between versions of the same compiler. That is exactly why the Bestiary is in your words: your entry has to say what the message meant, so it still works on a machine that words it differently. Paste the message in as well if you like, but the sentence that earns its place is yours.

One more line, at the front of the Bestiary, because today's cliff belongs in a different chapter. The int that wrapped was caught by nobody. It compiled, it ran, it printed a number, and the number was wrong. Write that down where you will see it again.
